section.heading: 3.4. The Chain Rule
section.paragraph: Suppose you are asked to differentiate the function
The differentiation formulas you learned in the previous sections of this chapter do not enable you to calculate $$F^{\prime}(x)$$ .

Observe that $$F$$ is a composite function. In fact, if we let $$y = {f(u)} = \sqrt{u}$$ and let $$u = {g(x)} = x^{2} + 1$$ , then we can write $$y = {F(x)} = {f({g(x)})}$$ , that is, $$F = f \circ g$$ . We know how to differentiate both $$f$$ and $$g$$ , so it would be useful to have a rule that tells us how to find the derivative of $$F = f \circ g$$ in terms of the derivatives of $$f$$ and $$g$$ .
See Section 1.3 for a review of composite functions.
section.heading: The Chain Rule
section.paragraph: It turns out that the derivative of the composite function $$f \circ g$$ is the product of the derivatives of $$f$$ and $$g$$ . This fact is one of the most important of the differentiation rules and is called the Chain Rule. It seems plausible if we interpret derivatives as rates of change. Regard $$\mathit{du} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ as the rate of change of $$u$$ with respect to $$x$$ , $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{du}$$ as the rate of change of $$y$$ with respect to $$u$$ , and $$\mathit{dy} \slash \mathit{dx}$$ as the rate of change of $$y$$ with respect to $$x$$ . If $$u$$ changes twice as fast as $$x$$ and $$y$$ changes three times as fast as $$u$$ , then it seems reasonable that $$y$$ changes six times as fast as $$x$$ , and so we expect that $$dy/dx$$ is the product of $$dy/du$$ and $$du/dx$$ .

section.paragraph: In Example 2(a) we combined the Chain Rule with the rule for differentiating the sine function. In general, if $$y = \sin u$$ , where $$u$$ is a differentiable function of $$x$$ , then, by the Chain Rule,
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = \cos u\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}$$
Thus
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({\sin u})} = \cos u\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}}$$
In a similar fashion, all of the formulas for differentiating trigonometric functions can be combined with the Chain Rule.

Let’s make explicit the special case of the Chain Rule where the outer function $$f$$ is a power function. If $$y = {\lbrack{g(x)}\rbrack}^{n}$$ , then we can write $$y = {f(u)} = u^{n}$$ where $$u = {g(x)}$$ . By using the Chain Rule and then the Power Rule, we get
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = nu^{n - 1}\frac{\mathit{du}}{\mathit{dx}} = n{\lbrack{g(x)}\rbrack}^{n - 1}{g^{\prime}(x)}$$

section.heading: How to Prove the Chain Rule
section.paragraph: Recall that if $$y = {f(x)}$$ and $$x$$ changes from $$a$$ to $$a + \Delta x$$ , we define the increment of $$y$$ as
$$\Delta y = {f({a + \Delta x})} - {f(a)}$$
According to the definition of a derivative, we have
$$\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = {f^{\prime}(a)}$$
So if we denote by $$\varepsilon$$ the difference between $$\Delta y/\Delta x$$ and $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ , we obtain
$$\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\varepsilon = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\left( {\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} - {f^{\prime}(a)}} \right) = {f^{\prime}(a)} - {f^{\prime}(a)} = 0$$
But
$$\left. {\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} - {f^{\prime}(a)}} \Rightarrow {\Delta y = {f^{\prime}(a)}\Delta x + \varepsilon\Delta x} \right.$$
If we define $$\varepsilon$$ to be $$0$$ when $$\Delta x = 0$$ , then $$\varepsilon$$ becomes a continuous function of $$\Delta x$$ . Thus, for a differentiable function $$f$$ , we can write
$${\Delta y = {f^{\prime}(a)}\Delta x + \varepsilon\Delta x} \text{where} \left. \varepsilon\rightarrow 0{as}\Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$
and $$\varepsilon$$ is a continuous function of $$\Delta x$$ . This property of differentiable functions is what enables us to prove the Chain Rule.
section.heading: Proof of the Chain Rule
section.paragraph: Suppose $$u = {g(x)}$$ is differentiable at $$a$$ and $$y = {f(u)}$$ is differentiable at $$b = {g(a)}$$ . If $$\Delta x$$ is an increment in $$x$$ and $$\Delta u$$ and $$\Delta y$$ are the corresponding increments in $$u$$ and $$y$$ , then we can use Equation 6 to write
$$\Delta u = {g^{\prime}(a)}\Delta x + \varepsilon_{1}\Delta x = {\lbrack{{g^{\prime}(a)} + \varepsilon_{1}}\rbrack}\Delta x$$
where $$\left. \varepsilon_{1}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . Similarly
$$\Delta y = {f^{\prime}(b)}\Delta u + \varepsilon_{2}\Delta u = {\lbrack{{f^{\prime}(b)} + \varepsilon_{2}}\rbrack}\Delta u$$
where $$\left. \varepsilon_{2}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. \Delta u\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . If we now substitute the expression for $$\Delta u$$ from Equation 7 into Equation 8, we get
$$\Delta y = {\lbrack{{f^{\prime}(b)} + \varepsilon_{2}}\rbrack}{\lbrack{{g^{\prime}(a)} + \varepsilon_{1}}\rbrack}\Delta x$$
so
$$\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = {\lbrack{{f^{\prime}(b)} + \varepsilon_{2}}\rbrack}{\lbrack{{g^{\prime}(a)} + \varepsilon_{1}}\rbrack}$$
As $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , Equation 7 shows that $$\left. \Delta u\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . Taking the limit as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}(b)} + \varepsilon_{2}}\rbrack}{\lbrack{{g^{\prime}(a)} + \varepsilon_{1}}\rbrack}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} = {{f^{\prime}(b)}{g^{\prime}(a)} = {f^{\prime}({g(a)})}{g^{\prime}(a)}}} \end{array}$$
This proves the Chain Rule.

note.title: James Gregory
note.heading: James Gregory
note.paragraph: The first person to formulate the Chain Rule was the Scottish mathematician James Gregory (1638–1675), who also designed the first practical reflecting telescope. Gregory discovered the basic ideas of calculus at about the same time as Newton. He became the first Professor of Mathematics at the University of St. Andrews and later held the same position at the University of Edinburgh. But one year after accepting that position, he died at the age of 36.
